top_story: By 26 October, the Yemen war had sharpened on both sides of the Saudi border as the Houthis claimed strikes on the East-West crude oil pumping network and Riyadh airport, signaling a willingness to hit economic infrastructure and civilian transit deep inside the kingdom. The immediate regional risk is not only tighter pressure on oil flows, but a wider conflict space in which energy systems and transport hubs become bargaining tools. Inside Yemen, that escalation sits atop a far older emergency: fuel shortages in besieged Taiz have pushed hospitals to the edge, cutting incubator capacity from 40 to 10 and exposing newborns to lethal cold. Tehran’s March threat to answer pressure on its own energy infrastructure with regional escalation underscores the broader pattern that infrastructure warfare is increasingly binding frontline combat to civilian suffering and cross-border economic vulnerability.
